passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: Text A: A Calendar Set by a Fish
passage_parts.text: The Tao people of Lanyu, a small island off the southeast coast of Taiwan, organize their year around the flying fish. Their traditional calendar divides the year into three seasons, each defined by the flying fish harvest. When the coral trees on the island burst into bloom, usually around February, the Kuroshio Current carries flying fish into the surrounding waters. Each village then gathers on the shore for a ceremony to call the fish, which marks the start of the fishing season. Until about June, the men catch flying fish and other fish that pass through the area, but they leave the fish living on the coral reefs alone, while the women clean and dry the catch. From about July to September, when the flying fish have gone, reef fish may be caught again. The quiet months from November to January are spent waiting for the fish to return. By setting limits on what may be caught and when, the calendar gives the reef fish several months of rest each year. According to Taiwan's Marine National Park Headquarters, this has helped many species around the island survive and reproduce.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Text B: A Visitor’s Notes from Lanyu
passage_parts.text:
I arrived on Lanyu in early May, right in the middle of the flying fish season. Along the beach, wooden boats painted with red, white and black patterns were lined up on the sand. Our guide, a young Tao man, asked us not to climb onto them to take photos, since the boats are treated with great respect at this time of year. He also reminded us not to bring oranges to the seaside until the season was over. I did not understand why, but I left mine at the guesthouse.
On my second day, I asked him whether we could join a fishing trip near the coral reefs. He smiled and said we would have to come back in the summer. That evening, he showed us rows of flying fish drying on racks outside his family's home and explained how they would be stored for the months ahead. By the time I left, I realized that on Lanyu, even a visitor's plans are shaped by the movements of a fish.

translation_zh.text:
達悟族的飛魚曆

【文本 A：由魚決定的曆法】
住在蘭嶼（台灣東南外海的一座小島）的達悟族，依照飛魚來安排他們的一年。他們的傳統曆法依飛魚的漁獲把一年分成三個季節。

當島上的刺桐花盛開，通常在二月左右，黑潮就把飛魚帶進周圍的海域。接著每個部落都會聚集在岸邊舉行招魚的儀式，宣告漁季開始。直到大約六月，男人捕捉飛魚和其他洄游經過的魚，但不去碰住在珊瑚礁上的魚，而女人則負責清理並曬乾漁獲。大約七月到九月，飛魚離開之後，才可以再捕礁岩魚。十一月到一月這段寧靜的月份，則是在等待飛魚回來。

藉由限制可以捕什麼、什麼時候捕，這套曆法讓礁岩魚每年都有好幾個月的休養。根據台灣的海洋國家公園管理處，這幫助了島上周圍許多物種存活與繁衍。

【文本 B：一位遊客的蘭嶼筆記】
我在五月初抵達蘭嶼，正是飛魚季進行得如火如荼的時候。沙灘上排列著漆有紅、白、黑花紋的木船。我們的導遊是一位年輕的達悟族男子，他請我們不要爬上船拍照，因為在一年中的這個時候，船是受到高度尊重的。他也提醒我們，在漁季結束前不要把橘子帶到海邊。我不懂為什麼，但還是把我的橘子留在民宿。

第二天，我問他我們能不能參加到珊瑚礁附近的捕魚行程。他笑著說，我們得夏天再來才行。那天傍晚，他帶我們看他家門外一排排架子上曬著的飛魚，並解釋接下來的幾個月要怎麼保存它們。等到我離開時，我才體會到，在蘭嶼，就連遊客的計畫都受到一種魚的動向左右。

open_tasks.prompt: Make a simple comparison of the two texts. For each text, write one English sentence about (1) who is speaking and (2) what the text tells us about catching reef fish.
reference_answers: Text A: An outside writer explains the Tao calendar; it says reef fish are left alone during the flying fish season and caught again from about July to September.
Text B: A visitor describes a trip in May; the guide says the group must come back in summer to fish near the reefs, which matches the rule in Text A.
